title: LZ's One Unexplained Recoil
hook: The world's most sensitive dark matter detector widened its search window and found exactly one hard nuclear recoil where almost no background should be. Not a discovery — but not nothing either.
key_points: LUX-ZEPLIN reported 2.84 tonne-years of xenon exposure, extending the nuclear-recoil window up to about 270 keV.
The wider window targets effective-field-theory and inelastic dark matter models, which predict harder recoils than the standard case.
One event was seen at 248 keV, with statistical and systematic uncertainties of about 23 keV each.
The known background expectation in that region is low, so a single event is already notable.
Tension with background-only is 2.6 sigma globally after the look-elsewhere effect, and up to 3.4 sigma locally.
Well short of the 5 sigma bar for discovery — the collaboration presents it as an event of interest, not a signal.
content_html: The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment sits deep underground in South Dakota watching seven tonnes of liquid xenon for the tiny recoil a dark matter particle would leave behind. In a new analysis, the collaboration pushed its search up to roughly 270 keV of recoil energy — much harder than the usual hunting ground — and found a single event at 248 keV in a region where essentially no background was expected.
extra_html: The extended window is not arbitrary. Standard spin-independent dark matter scattering piles up at low recoil energies, but effective-field-theory and inelastic models predict a much larger high-energy tail, so a search that stops early would simply miss them. Using 2.84 tonne-years of exposure, LZ found one event at 248 +/- 23 (stat) +/- 23 (sys) keV. A profile likelihood ratio test puts the tension with a background-only universe at 2.6 sigma globally once the look-elsewhere effect is accounted for, with a maximum local significance of 3.4 sigma across the models tested. The paper spends most of its length on the background model and the rare topologies — cosmogenic, radiogenic, and detector-edge effects — that could fake such a recoil. Theorists have already started proposing interpretations, but at this significance the honest reading is that one odd event turned up and more exposure will settle it.

related.title: Could One Odd Recoil Be a Higgsino?
related.hook: LUX-ZEPLIN saw a single 248 keV nuclear recoil it couldn't explain away. Two theorists point out that a TeV-mass Higgsino would produce exactly that kind of event — with no free parameters to tune.

related.title: The Sun Says No to the Higgsino Explanation
related.hook: If a Higgsino caused LZ's odd recoil, the Sun would have been quietly hoovering up dark matter for billions of years — and IceCube would see the neutrinos. It doesn't.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: A Dark Matter Detector That Asks Which Way the Hit Came From
related.hook: Neutrons and dark matter can leave identical-looking recoils. MIMAC's answer: reconstruct the direction of each recoil and check whether it points where dark matter should come from.

flashcards.prompt: Why did LZ extend its nuclear-recoil energy window to about 270 keV?
flashcards.back_html: Because effective-field-theory and inelastic dark matter models put a larger share of their predicted recoils at high energy than the standard spin-independent case does.

flashcards.prompt: How strong is the evidence from LZ's 248 keV event?

choices.text: 2.6 sigma globally — interesting, but far below the discovery threshold
5 sigma — a confirmed dark matter detection
Zero — the event is fully explained by known backgrounds

flashcards.explanation_html: The global significance is 2.6 sigma after accounting for the look-elsewhere effect (3.4 sigma local at most). Particle physics reserves "discovery" for 5 sigma.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 'look-elsewhere effect' correct for?
flashcards.back_html: For the fact that you searched many models and energy regions. Some fluctuation somewhere is likely by chance, so the local significance must be deflated to a smaller global one.
